summary: IKEv2 normally requires that the responder prove its identity using a public key signature even when EAP is used for the client. This document defines an extension allowing EAP methods that already provide mutual authentication and key agreement to be used on their own, skipping the signature step.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally a server has to show an official ID card even when you and it have already proved who you are some other way. This lets them skip the extra ID check when the first way was strong enough.

questions: what is eap only authentication in ikev2
how does ikev2 skip the responder signature
which eap methods are safe for ikev2 eap only
subtitle: Lets IKEv2 authenticate the gateway with a strong EAP method alone, without a public key signature.

tldr.problem: IKEv2 requires the responder to authenticate with a public key signature even when a mutually authenticating EAP method is used. That demands a PKI and trust anchor management on every client, which is often unrealistic.
tldr.mechanism: The initiator adds an EAP_ONLY_AUTHENTICATION notification (16417) to its first IKE_AUTH message. If the responder agrees, it omits its AUTH and CERT payloads, and the IKE SA is authenticated by AUTH payloads based on the EAP-generated key.
tldr.outcome: Only EAP methods that are mutually authenticating, key-generating and dictionary-attack resistant may be used. The RFC updates RFC 5996.

today: RFC 5998 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 5996. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why EAP-Only Authentication
sections.content:
IKEv2 is part of IPsec and sets up Security Associations. It supports public key signatures, shared secrets and EAP (Extensible Authentication Protocol). EAP lets IKEv2 reuse existing credential databases and lets the VPN gateway be separate from a backend AAA server.

Older EAP methods authenticate only the client, so IKEv2 pairs them with a public key signature from the responder. Newer methods, such as those used with IEEE 802.11i, give mutual authentication and key agreement, yet IKEv2 still requires the signature. That needs a PKI with trust anchors on all supplicants, which the RFC says is often not realistic. This document lets such methods provide responder authentication completely through EAP.
sections.plainLanguage: If two people already proved who they are with a strong secret, making the host also show an ID card is extra work, especially if nobody can check ID cards anyway.

sections.title: Deployment Scenarios
sections.content:
Two illustrative scenarios are given. In the first, the EAP server and the IKEv2 responder are co-located. Authenticating the responder with both EAP and a signature is redundant, and EAP offers many methods with different properties, such as strong password-based protocols.

In the second, a corporate VPN gateway is the IKEv2 responder and the EAP conversation runs between the client and a home AAA server. Session keys are sent from the AAA server to the gateway, using for example Diameter or RADIUS, and are then used to authenticate the IKEv2 SA with AUTH payloads.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the guard at the door checks your secret handshake himself. Sometimes he phones the head office to check it for him.

sections.title: The Extension
sections.content:
An initiator that does not want public-key responder authentication includes an EAP_ONLY_AUTHENTICATION notification payload (16417) in message 3, the first IKE_AUTH request. Protocol ID and SPI size are zero and there is no extra data. If the responder supports and accepts it, it omits the public-key AUTH and CERT payloads from message 4. Otherwise it ignores the notification and includes the AUTH payload, and the initiator MUST verify it as usual.

The initiator MUST verify that the EAP method is allowed by this specification and abort immediately if not. Both sides MUST check that the method gave mutual authentication and a shared secret key. The AUTH payloads after EAP Success MUST use the EAP-generated key and MUST NOT use SK_pi or SK_pr.

A session set up with this extension can be resumed using RFC 5723, but the initiator MUST NOT send the extension during the IKE_AUTH of the resumed session.
sections.plainLanguage: The visitor says up front that he will skip the ID card and rely on the handshake. If the host agrees, they continue. If not, the usual ID check happens. Either way, a final secret handshake seals the deal.

sections.title: Safe EAP Methods
sections.content:
Any EAP method used with this extension MUST be mutually authenticating, key-generating and resistant to dictionary attacks. The authors list methods they believe are safe, noting the list is not inclusive: EAP-SIM, EAP-AKA, EAP-AKA', EAP-GPSK, EAP-pwd, EAP-EKE, EAP-PAX, EAP-SAKE, EAP-SRP, EAP-POTP (mutual variant), EAP-TLS, EAP-FAST and EAP-TTLS.

The table also marks whether each allows channel binding, where protected identity information passes between the EAP endpoints. This optional property helps against certain attacks, so in some scenarios such methods are preferred. The RFC notes that no RFC specifies which identities should be sent under that protection or what policy correlates identities at different layers.
sections.plainLanguage: Not every secret handshake is good enough. It has to work both ways, produce a shared secret, and not be guessable by trying lots of words.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Running an EAP conversation alone does not authenticate the IKEv2 SA. The crucial step is the AUTH payload based on the EAP-generated key, so methods without mutual authentication or a shared key MUST NOT be used.

With a backend AAA server there are two authentications: client to AAA server, and AAA server to gateway. Some EAP methods do not identify the gateway, so a client only learns it is talking to some gateway trusted by the home AAA server, and a compromised gateway could impersonate others. This is called the Lying NAS Problem, and channel binding is the mitigation. AAA proxies MUST be trusted and SHOULD be avoided when possible.

EAP payloads are protected by SK_e and SK_a, but until the AUTH payload is verified a man-in-the-middle can alter KEi/KEr and read or modify EAP payloads. Methods vulnerable to dictionary attacks stay vulnerable to active attackers inside IKEv2, which is why Section 4 sets its rules. IKEv2 protects the initiator's identity against passive eavesdroppers only, and EAP-only use cannot guarantee protection of the responder's identity.
sections.plainLanguage: The handshake itself is not what proves things. The final sealed note, made with the handshake's secret, is. And if the guard trusts a head office, a dishonest guard could pretend to be another guard.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The document defines a new IKEv2 Notification Payload type, EAP_ONLY_AUTHENTICATION. It has been assigned type number 16417 from the Status Types range.
sections.plainLanguage: The new message got its own official number so everyone recognizes it.
